title: Ireland
description: Island in the North Atlantic Ocean
wiki_lead:
Ireland is an island in the North Atlantic Ocean, in Northwestern Europe. Geopolitically, the island is divided between the Republic of Ireland (officially named Ireland – a sovereign state covering five-sixths of the island) and Northern Ireland (part of the United Kingdom – covering the remaining sixth). It is separated from Great Britain to its east by the North Channel, the Irish Sea, and St George's Channel. Ireland is the second-largest island of the British Isles, the third-largest in Europe, and the twentieth-largest in the world. As of 2022, the island's population is just over 7 million, with 5.1 million in the Republic of Ireland and 1.9 million in Northern Ireland, making it the second-most populous island in Europe after Great Britain.
Ireland's geography comprises relatively low-lying mountains surrounding a central plain, with several navigable rivers extending inland. Much of Ireland was woodland until the end of the Middle Ages. Today, woodland makes up about 10% of the island, compared with a European average of over 33%, with most of it being non-native conifer plantations. Its lush vegetation is a product of its mild climate, which is influenced by the Atlantic Ocean and thus very moderate, and winters are milder than expected for such a northerly area, although summers are cooler than those in continental Europe. Rainfall and cloud cover are abundant.
Gaelic Ireland had emerged by the 1st century AD. The island was Christianised from the 5th century onwards. During this period, Ireland was divided amongst petty kings, who in turn served under the kings of the traditional provinces (Cúige; lit. 'fifth') vying for dominance and the title of High King of Ireland. Between the late 8th and early 11th centuries, Viking raids and settlement took place, culminating in the Battle of Clontarf on 23 April 1014, which resulted in the decline of Viking power in Ireland. Following the 12th-century Anglo-Norman invasion, England claimed sovereignty. However, English rule did not extend over the whole island until the 16th–17th century Tudor conquest, which led to colonisation by settlers from Britain. In the 1690s, a system of Protestant English rule was designed to materially disadvantage the Catholic majority and Protestant dissenters, and was extended during the 18th century. With the Acts of Union in 1801, Ireland became a part of the United Kingdom. The Great Famine of the 1840s saw the population fall by over 20%, through death and emigration. A war of independence in the early 20th century was followed by the partition of the island, leading to the creation of the Irish Free State, which became increasingly sovereign over the following decades until it declared a republic in 1949 (Republic of Ireland Act, 1948) and Northern Ireland, which remained a part of the United Kingdom. Northern Ireland saw much civil unrest from the late 1960s until the 1990s. This subsided following the Good Friday Agreement in 1998. In 1973, both the Republic of Ireland and the United Kingdom, with Northern Ireland as part of it, joined the European Economic Community. Following a referendum vote in 2016, the United Kingdom, including Northern Ireland, left the European Union (EU) in 2020. Northern Ireland was granted a limited special status and allowed to operate within the EU single market for goods without being in the European Union.
Irish culture has had an influence on other cultures, particularly in literature. Alongside mainstream Western culture, an indigenous culture exists, as expressed through Gaelic games, Irish folk music, Irish language, and Irish dance. The island's culture shares many features with that of Great Britain, including the English language, and sports such as association football, rugby, horse racing, golf, and boxing.

grok_lead: Ireland is an island lying in the North Atlantic Ocean west of Great Britain, geopolitically divided between the independent Republic of Ireland, which comprises five-sixths of the island, and Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom. The Republic of Ireland is a parliamentary republic in northwestern Europe with a land area of 70,273 square kilometers and a population estimated at 5.38 million as of April 2024. Northern Ireland, a devolved part of the United Kingdom, has a land area of 14,148 square kilometers and a population estimated at 1.93 million as of mid-2024. Together, the island has a land area of 84,421 square kilometers and a population of approximately 7.31 million as of 2024. The capital and largest city of the Republic of Ireland, Dublin, serves as the political, economic, and cultural center, housing over one-third of the Republic's residents in its metropolitan area and extending as a cultural and economic center for the entire island through initiatives such as the Dublin-Belfast Economic Corridor. Belfast is the capital and largest city of Northern Ireland. Governed as a unitary parliamentary democracy, the Republic elects a president as ceremonial head of state for a seven-year term and a taoiseach (prime minister) as head of government, with legislative power vested in the Oireachtas comprising DÃ¡il Ãireann and Seanad Ãireann. Northern Ireland operates a devolved government within the United Kingdom, with legislative power in the Northern Ireland Assembly (90 members) and executive authority in the Northern Ireland Executive, jointly headed by the First Minister and deputy First Minister. The island's geography features a central plain surrounded by mountains and bogs, with a temperate maritime climate influenced by the Gulf Stream, supporting agriculture dominated by livestock such as dairy cattle and sheep. Historically shaped by Celtic settlement around 500 BCE, successive invasions by Vikings, Normans, and English forces led to centuries of colonial rule, culminating in partial independence via the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty after the War of Independence, though partition created Northern Ireland amid ensuing civil conflict. Economically, Ireland transitioned from agrarian poverty in the mid-20th century to one of Europe's wealthiest states by attracting foreign direct investment through low corporate taxes and EU single-market access, recording GDP growth of 2.6% in 2024 with gross national income* rising 4.8% the same year, reflecting stronger domestic activity as multinational effects did not inflate headline GDP figures in this year. This model has drawn criticism for exacerbating housing shortages and regional inequalities, as domestic demand indicators like modified gross domestic product reveal less robust underlying activity. Culturally, Ireland's global influence stems from its literary tradition, including Nobel laureates like Yeats and Beckett, and a diaspora exceeding 70 million descendants worldwide, forged by events such as the 19th-century Great Famine.
